On Feb 26, 1:41 pm, Matt Giovanni <matthewgiova...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi everyone-
>
> To begin with, I'd like to thank Andy, Ian, Richard, Elise for
> developing this modeling package for R.  It's a fantastic resource for
> ecologists like myself that do not have a lot of programming skills.
> I also want to thank Ian for his input thus far and for facilitating
> discussion on Unmarked and the models therein.
>

Glad you're enjoying unmarked!

> I'm trying to assess goodness-of-fit for a set of n-mix abundance
> models, and have followed the example of parametric bootstrapping in
> the Unmarked overview/tutorial.  My understanding is that each MC
> simulation produces a mean squared error value for comparison with the
> MSE value from the original model.  Is this accurate?

This is nearly correct -- we're comparing root-mean-squared error
(RMSE), though the difference shouldn't matter.

> The MSE's are
> then plotted into a histogram, and, this is where I am more unclear,
> the original MSE is compared to the distribution of the simulated
> MSE's with a t-test to produce a p-value?
>

The p-value is just a bootstrap estimate of the probability of RMSE
being larger than the observed one under the null hypothesis that the
fitted model is correct.  So it can be interpreted similarly to a chi-
square GOF p-value, but there is no parametric distribution (chi-
square, t, normal) being used to compute the p-value.  It comes
directly from the bootstrap distribution.

Hope that helps,
Ian

messages.subject: unmarked 0.8-3 released
messages.body_plain:
Hi unmarkedsters,

I'm pleased to announce the release of unmarked 0.8-3.  A full list of
changes can be found by reviewing the commit history at
http://github.com/ianfiske/unmarked.  The most important new features
are:

1.  Non-parametric boostrapping can now be used to derive standard
errors for any of the unmarked model fits or subsequent linearComb()
and backTransform() estimates.  For example, continuing from the
occu() example as so:

> example(occu)
> fm <- nonparboot(fm, B = 50)
> vcov(fm, method = "nonparboot")
> SE(fm, method = "nonparboot")
> det.at.obshalf <- backTransform(linearComb(fm, type = "det", c(1, 0.5)))
> SE(det.at.obshalf)

2.  You can now compute both smoothed and projected trajectories from
colext() model fits.  Simply use smoothed(fm) or projected(fm) to
extract trajectories.  You can also compute standard errors for these
quantities with a non-parametric bootstrap:

> example(colext)
> fm <- nonparboot(fm, B = 50) ## this is slow!
> smoothed(fm)
> f...@smoothed.mean.bsse ## get the bootstrap standard error

Best,
Ian

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I'm wondering how unmarked and the PRESENCE software (
http://www.mbr-pwrc.usgs.gov/software/doc/presence/presence.html )
compare.

For example, I just tried a couple of models using the wt data
provided with unmarked (widewt.csv) in both unmarked and PRESENCE
(i.e. I used exactly the same data in both software). I just tested
single variable models (I don't know much - anything really - about
the data so am not sure how sensble these models are from an
ecological perspective). Here are the model comparison tables (hope
the formatting survives):

i) unmarked

		n	nPars	AIC		deltaAIC	AICwt
Elev		237	3		496.51	0		9.72E-01
forest	237	3	        503.63	7.1261	2.76E-02
date		237	3		529.69	33.1812	6.06E-08
ivel		237	3		529.98	33.4725	5.24E-08
length	237	3		530.7	34.1937	3.65E-08

ii) PRESENCE

Model	        AIC	        deltaAIC	AIC wgt	Model Likelihood	no.Par.
psi(elev),p(.)	515.63	0	        0.9969	1	        2
psi(forest),p(.)	528.49	12.86	0.0016	0.0016	2
psi(length),p(.)	528.64	13.01	0.0015	0.0015	2
psi(.),p(ivel)	563.44	47.81	0	        0	        2
psi(.),p(date)	582.21	66.58	0	        0	        2

Although some variation in AIC might be expected due to the specifics
of different algorithms in R vs PRESENCE I am surprised that the
length variable goes from being 'worst' model (according to AIC) in
unmarked to third ranked model in PRESENCE (although elevation is
clearly best performing model according to AIC in both cases).

Could someone shed some light on why this might be? Am I incorrect to
assume that results for unmarked and PRESENCE for the same data should
be very similar?

I found similar differences between models in unmarked and PRESENCE
for my own data. It's great to see this modelling capability now
available in R - just need to understand better how it compares to
what other software is doing...

Thanks for your help,

James

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am using the unmarked package for a little while now and am very
happy with it, so thank you very much for all the effort you put into
that.

Now to my problem:

The model function I use is occu. So far I have used precreated model
sets like:

occu1<- occu(~1 ~near_frshwZ+UTM_E_UTM_N+FOR1_DA_100Z+FOR_1KZ, UMF)
occu2<- occu(~1 ~near_frshwZ+UTM_E_UTM_N+FOR1_DA_100Z+FOR_1KZ

before doing

fitList()
and
modSel()

to rank the models used (before averaging them).

Right now I am trying to make a stepwise routine for model selection
using occu. The stepwise function I am editing is already working well
with functions from the lme4 package like lmer. I am running into some
very strange problems with occu though, which is the reason I am
posting here.

Now my null model is something like the following with a couple of
variables for both the detectability as well as the occupancy side:

BRCR<- occu(~ Lndar_1kmZ + FOR1_DA_1KZ + CR_CL_3Z + DATE_JUL + OCODES
~ rdl_up_100Z +  FOR0_100Z +  FOR1_DA_100Z +  CR_CL0Z +  CR_CL_3Z +
OF_100Z + DATE_JUL, UMF)

What the stepwise function is doing (or should do) is trying to remove

Error in parse(text = x) : unexpected symbol in:

For some strange reason the function tries to put the detectability

The thing I can think of that might produce a problem is with the two

If you have any other suggestions on the matter I would be very
grateful as this error is really puzzling me and being fairly new to R

hi Jami,
 you should try to read your data set into R wth read.csv and see if it coereces all of the variables to factors. [can you provide your data set for me to look at?].

The default parameterization is log(E[N]) and logit(p) (Ian can correct me if thats wrong).  So you need to exp() the intercept to get "individuals per location" and
exp(intercept)/(1+exp(intercept)) to get the baseline detection probability.  This is why negative estimates are allowed.

regards,
andy

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] occu function
messages.body_plain:
Hi Richard,

Glad you're happy with unmarked!

I think that you're right that the problem is most likely because of the double RH-sided formula that unmarked uses.  Any general code from another R package would need to be adapted to handle this and I would be surprised if any such code worked without careful adaptation!

That said, I don't have time to adapt it myself immediately, but it's on the to-do and anyone else is welcome to contribute such a thing!  I would suggest playing around with creating formulas as character strings through whatever means is necessary (likely with paste()), and then coercing to a formula with as.formula().  Another approach would be to write a small wrapper for occu() that had the desired input formula structure (2 formulas) and that calls unmarked's occu().  This might be easier to adapt the existing stepwise code.

I hope that helps,
Ian

(ypm) 1-7 as a-g in the csv.  The other problem I had was correctly
distinguishing the site- and obs-level covariates in the umf, so I
reformatted my csv files to "wide" format, like the widewt example
file in the csv folder of Unmarked, and then everything worked fine.

### load Unmarked package
library(unmarked)
### select a species csv datafile for abundance modeling and convert

umf=csvToUMF("BOBO SK.csv",long=FALSE,type="unmarkedFramePCount")
### summarize model variables in umf
summary(umf)
### Observer-specific detection parameter, mng type and ypm abundance

year=pcount(~obs ~year+offset(log(area)),umf)
mng=pcount(~obs ~mng+year+offset(log(area)),umf)

global=pcount(~obs ~mng+ypm+year+offset(log(area)),umf)
models=fitList(year,mng,ypm,global)
modSel(models)
summary(global)

obsCovs(umf) <- cbind(obsCovs(umf), year = as.factor(rep(rep(1:T, each = J), M))
